FOREWORD 


This Indian Standard (Part 58) (Second Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft 
finalized by the Water Quality Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 


The chemical oxygen demand (COD) determines the amount of oxygen required for the chemical oxidation of 
organic matter using a strong chemical oxidant, such as potassium dichromate under reflux conditions. The COD 
determination in water and wastewater is widely used to determine the following: 


a) Degree of pollution in water bodies and their self-purification capacity; 
b) Efficiency of treatment plants; 
c) Pollution loads; and 


d) Provides rough idea of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) which can be used to determine sample 
volume for BOD estimation. 


The limitation of the test lies in its inability to differentiate between the biologically oxidizable and biologically 
inert material. COD determination has an advantage over biological oxygen demand (BOD) test in that the results 
can be obtained in less than 5 h whereas BOD determination requires 3 or 5 days. Further the test is relatively 
easy and precise. Also there are not many interferences as in the case of BOD. 


The Committee responsible for formulation of IS 3025 : 1964 ‘Methods of sampling and test (physical and 
chemical) for water used in industry’ decided to revise the standard and publish it in separate parts. This standard 
superseded 4 of IS 2488 (Part 5) : 1976 'Methods of sampling and test for industrial effluents, Part 5' and 52 of 
IS 3025 : 1964 'Methods of sampling and test (physical and chemical) for water used in industry’ and was one 
among the different parts published under IS 3025 series of standards. The first revision of this standard was 
published in 2006. 


In this second revision the following modification have been made: 
a) The method for determination of COD has been updated. 


In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from the method No. 5520 B 
of — Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater, published by the American Public Health 
Association, Washington, USA, 23nd Edition, 2017. 


The composition of the Committee responsible for the formulation of this standard is given in Annex A. 


In reporting the results of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 2022 ‘Rules for rounding off numerical 
values (second revision)’. 


IS 3025 (Part 58) : 2023 


Indian Standard 


METHODS OF SAMPLING AND TEST (PHYSICAL AND 
CHEMICAL) FOR WATER AND WASTEWATER 


PART 58 CHEMICAL OXYGEN DEMAND (COD) 


( Second Revision ) 


1 SCOPE 


This standard (Part 58) prescribes the open reflux 
method for determination of chemical oxygen 
demand (COD) in water and wastewater. 


2 REFERENCES 


The standards given below contain provisions which 
through reference in this text constitute provisions 
of this standard. At the time of publication, the 
editions indicated were valid. All standards are 
subject to revision and parties to agreements based 
on this standard are encouraged to investigate the 
possibility of applying the most recent editions of 
these standards: 


IS No. Title 


IS 7022 (Part 1): Glossary of terms relating to 
1973 water, sewage and industrial

IS 7022 (Part 2): Glossary of terms relating to

3 TERMINOLOGY 


For the purpose of this standard, definitions given in 
IS 7022 (Part 1) and IS 7022 (Part 2) shall apply. 


4 SAMPLING AND PRESERVATION 


Sampling and sample preservation shall be done as 
prescribed in IS 17614 (Part 3) 


5 PRINCIPLE 


Most of the organic matters are-destroyed when 
boiled with a mixture of potassium dichromate and 
sulphuric acid producing carbon dioxide and water. 
A sample is refluxed with a known amount of 
potassium dichromate in sulphuric acid medium and 
the excess of dichromate is titrated against ferrous 
ammonium sulphate. The amount of dichromate 
consumed is proportional to the oxygen required to 
oxidize the oxidizable organic matter. 


6 INTERFERENCE 


6.1 Straight-chain aliphatic compounds, aromatic 


hydrocarbon fatty acids, chlorides, nitrites and iron 
are the main interfering radicals. The interference 
caused by chlorides can be eliminated by the 
addition of mercuric sulphate to the sample prior to 
addition of other reagents. About 0.4 g mercuric 
sulphate (HgSO,) is adequate to complex 40 mg 
chloride (CI) ions in the form of poorly ionized 
mercuric chloride (HgC1). 


6.2 Nitrite exerts a COD of 1.1 mg/mg N, hence 
120 mg of sulphamic acid is added to potassium 
dichromate solution to avoid interference caused by 
nitrite (NO2). When 20 ml sample and 10 ml 
dichromate is taken, this can take care of 
concentrations up to 6 mg/l NO>-N. 


6.3 Silver sulphate is added to concentrated H2SO, 
(22 g/4 kg acid) as a catalyst. This accelerates the 
oxidation of straight-chain aliphatic and aromatic 
compounds. 


6.4 For complete and better oxidation of organic 
matter it is necessary to maintain the final 
concentration of H2SO, at 18 N. 


7 APPARATUS 
7.1 Reflux Apparatus 


Consisting of series of flat bottom, 150 ml to 250 ml 
capacity tubes with glass joint and a long condenser. 


7.2 Hot Plate 


A digester block on which a series of refluxing sets 
are connected to provide uniform heating to all the 
tubes. 


8 REAGENTS 


8.1 Standard Potassium dichromate (K2Cr207) 
— 0.25 N. Dissolve 12.259 g potassium dichromate 
previously dried at 150 °C for 2 h, in distilled water. 
Dilute to 1 litre. This is equal to 0.25 N Primary 
Standard. 


8.2 Sulphuric Acid, Concentrated 


Add 22 g silver sulphate to 4 kg (10.12 g silver 
sulphate/l) concentrated HSO, bottle. Keep 
overnight for dissolution. Shake well after 
dissolution. 


IS 3025 (Part 58) : 2023 


8.3 Standard Ferrous Ammonium Sulphate 
(FAS) [Fe(NH,)2(SO4)2. 6H20] — 0.25 N. Dissolve 
98 g Fe (NH4)2(SO 4). 6H20 in distilled water. Add 
20 ml concentrated H>SO4, cool, and dilute to 1 litre. 
Standardize this solution daily against standard. 


8.4 Ferroin Indicator 


Dissolve 1.485 g of  1,10-Phenanthroline 
monohydrate and 695 mg FeSO,. 7H2O in water and 
dilute to 100 ml. 


NOTE — Already prepared indictor is also available in the 
market. 


8.5 Mercuric Sulphate (HgSOs), Crystal. 
8.6 Sulphamic Acid 


Add 10 mg sulphamic acid for each mg of nitrite 
interference is present. Generally, nitrite ions are 
insignificant. 


8.7 Potassium Hydrogen Pthalate (KPH) 
Standard 


Lightly crush and dry KHP to constant weight at 
110 °C. Dissolve 425 mg of KHP in distilled water 
and dilute to 1 000 ml. This solution is stable for a 
week, when refrigerated. If visible biological growth 
is observed, discard the solution. Potassium 
hydrogen phthalate (KHP) has a theoretical COD of 
1.176 mg/ O>/ mg and this solution has a theoretical 
COD of 500 ug O2/ ml. Therefore, KHP is used as a 
standard solution to evaluate the method and the 
quality of reagents. 


9 PROCEDURE 
9.1 Procedure for High-COD Sample (2 50 mg/l) 


Place 0.4g HgSO; in a reflux tube. Add 20 ml or an 
aliquot of sample diluted to 20 ml with distilled 
water. Mix well, so that chlorides are converted into 
poorly ionized mercuric chloride. Add 10 ml 
standard K2Cr2O7 solution and then add slowly 
30 ml sulphuric acid which already containing silver 
sulphate. Mix well, if the colour turns green, take 
fresh sample with smaller aliquot. Final 
concentration of concentrated HSO, should be 
always 18 N. 


Connect the tubes to condensers and reflux for 2 h at 
150 °C +2 °C. Cool and wash down the condensers 
with 60 ml distilled water. Cool and titrate excess 
potassium dichromate against standard ferrous 
ammonium sulphate using 2 to 3 drops of ferroin as 
indicator. Near the end of the titration colour 
changes sharply from blue green to reddish brown. 
Reflux a reagent blank simultaneously without the 
sample, under identical conditions. 


NOTE—This slow addition along with swirling prevents 
loss of volatile materials such as fatty acids, in the sample 


9.2 Alternate Procedure for Low-COD Samples 
(<50 mg/1) 

The method is same as for the high-COD samples 
(see 9.1) except that the concentration of K2Cr207 
should be 0.025 N and the ferrous ammonium 
sulphate to be 0.025 N respectively. The same can 
be prepared by 10 times dilution of the standards 
prepared at 8.1 and 8.3. 


9,3 Standardization of Ferrous Ammonium 
Sulphate 


Measure exactly 20 ml to 25 ml (as per convenient 
pipette availability standard K2Cr2O7 solution to 
about 100 ml. Add 30 ml concentrated H>SO4, and 
cool. Add 3 to 4 drops of ferroin indicator and titrate 
with ferrous ammonium sulphate till the colour 
changes to wine red. 

V, x 0.0250

where

titrated, in ml; and

10 CALCULATION 


(B-S) x N x 8 000 


COD, mg Ol = 
Vo 


where 


B = volume of Fe (NH4)2 (S04)2 required far 
titration against the blank, in ml; 


S = volume of Fe (NH4)2 (SO4)2 required for 
titration against the sample, in ml; 

N = normality of Fe (NH4)2(SO4)2; and 

Vo= volume of sample taken for testing, in ml. 


11 EXPRESSION OE RESULTS 


Results are expressed as mg/l of Oz. Report to the 
nearest whole number. 


12 PRECISION AND ACCURACY 


Precision and accuracy both depends upon the COD 
value. For the high COD values (= 400 mg/1) 
precision up to 2 percent is expected horn a good 
analyst. As the COD value goes on decreasing, 
precision also become poorer and poorer that is 
percentage goes on increasing. 


Precision for the low COD samples maybe improved 
by using alternate method where diluted reagents are 
used. 


IS 3025 (Part 58) : 2023
